How to price a personal training package without losing money on it

A discounted package can guarantee revenue and still pay you worse per hour than charging full price one session at a time. The gap comes from two things a plain revenue comparison skips: what a makeup-owed policy does to hours actually worked, and what a flat facility fee does to a discounted rate.

The same client relationship, two pricing models

A trainer bills $75 per single session. The same trainer also sells a package of 10 sessions for $580 — a 22.67% discount off the single-session rate. About 10% of booked sessions are no-shows, a missed package session earns a free makeup rather than being forfeited, and the gym charges a flat $12 facility fee for every session actually delivered, package or not.

Pay-per-sessionPackage (makeup owed)
Client billings$675.00$580.00
Facility fee owed$108.00$120.00
Net take-home$567.00$460.00
Hours actually worked9.0010.00
Net effective hourly pay$63.00/hr$46.00/hr

Same client, same no-show rate, same facility fee. Charging full price per session and letting a no-show simply free that slot nets $17.00/hr more than selling the package at this discount with a makeup owed.

Waiving the makeup helps, but doesn't close the gap

Keep every number the same and change one thing: a missed package session is forfeited instead of made up. Net effective hourly pay on the package rises from $46.00/hr to $52.44/hr, because the package now frees the same hour a pay-per-session no-show would. It is still below the $63.00/hr of charging full price, because the discount and the flat facility fee still apply to every hour that does get worked.

Package policyHours workedNet effective hourly pay
Makeup owed on a miss10.00$46.00/hr
No makeup owed (forfeited)9.00$52.44/hr
Pay-per-session (for reference)9.00$63.00/hr

Solving for a target instead of guessing at a discount

Rather than pick a package price and see what it nets, this calculator solves for the price that clears a take-home target directly. At a $45/hr target, the same 10-session, makeup-owed, $12-flat-fee package would need to be priced at $570 — $10 less than the $580 in the worked example above, which already overshoots that target by a dollar. Change the rate, the no-show rate, the makeup policy, or the venue's cost structure, and the target price moves with it; there is no fixed rule of thumb that survives every one of those changing independently.

What this is not

This is arithmetic on the rates, discount, no-show rate, makeup policy, and venue cost you type, applied to one representative block of sessions. It does not track which specific client owes a makeup, does not schedule anything, and does not predict any one client's actual attendance. Replace every figure with your own before relying on either number.

It is hosted best-effort with no SLA: it may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Open the package pricing calculator to compare your own numbers.

Common questions

How do I price a personal training package so it doesn't cost me money?

Check two things a revenue-only comparison misses: whether your discount is deeper than your real no-show rate once a missed session earns a makeup (every hour still gets worked, at the discounted rate), and whether your gym or studio charges a flat per-session facility fee rather than a percentage cut (a flat fee is a bigger percentage bite out of a discounted package session than out of a full-price one). On this calculator's own worked example — a $75 session, a 10-for-$580 package, 10% no-shows, makeup owed, $12 flat facility fee — the package nets $46.00/hr against $63.00/hr charging full price per session.

Why does a makeup-owed policy turn a safe-looking discount into a loss?

Because a no-show that must be made up is not actually saved hours — it is deferred hours. Pay-per-session, a no-show simply frees that slot: 10% no-shows on 10 sessions means 9 hours worked. With a makeup owed, all 10 hours are eventually worked at the discounted rate. A 22.67% package discount sold to cover a 10% no-show rate ends up paid on every hour, not just the ones attended, which is deeper than the risk it was meant to price.

Why does a flat facility fee hurt a package more than full price?

A flat fee is the same dollar amount no matter what you billed the client. On the worked example, a $12 facility fee is 16% of a $75 full-price session but 20.69% of the $58 package-equivalent rate — the same fixed fee eats a bigger share of a lower price. A percentage revenue-share cut does not do this: it takes the same share of both, so it scales the comparison down without changing which pricing model wins.

Does waiving the makeup fix the problem?

It helps, but does not fully close the gap. On the same worked example, dropping the makeup obligation raises the package's net effective hourly pay from $46.00/hr to $52.44/hr — because a package no-show now frees the same hour a pay-per-session no-show would. It is still below the $63.00/hr of charging full price per session, because the flat facility fee and the discount itself still apply to every hour that is worked.

What package price would have hit a $45/hr take-home target instead?

$570 for the same 10-session, makeup-owed, $12-flat-fee package — $10 less than the $580 in the worked example, because $580 already overshoots a $45/hr target by a dollar. This is not a rule of thumb; it is solved directly from your own rate, no-show rate, makeup policy and venue cost each time you run the calculator, since every one of those numbers changes the answer.

PERSONAL TRAINER PACKAGE PRICING CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Your package protects revenue. Does it protect your take-home pay?

A discounted prepaid session package guarantees you get paid even if a client no-shows. If a missed session also earns a free makeup rather than being forfeited, you still work that hour eventually — and if your gym or studio charges a flat per-session fee rather than a percentage cut, that fee does not shrink with your discount, so it takes a bigger bite out of a discounted package session than a full-price one. This calculator compares your package to plain pay-per-session pricing on net take-home pay per hour, after your venue's cut, so you know which one you are actually choosing.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Compare package vs. pay-per-session

Enter your single-session rate, a package size and price, then click Compare.

Comparison

Pricing modelNet take-homeHours workedNet effective pay

Copies both models' net revenue, hours, and net effective hourly pay, the deltas, and the disclaimer as plain text.

What this does and doesn't do

This applies the numbers you enter to one representative block of sessions — it does not track which specific client owes a makeup, does not schedule anything, and does not predict any one client's actual attendance. Treat the result as the arithmetic behind a pricing decision, not a record of any real client's account.

Common questions

Does a prepaid client package actually protect my income?

It protects your revenue: the client has already paid, so a no-show does not cost you that session's fee. It does not automatically protect your net take-home per hour. If your package promises a makeup for a missed session, you still work that hour eventually — the discount you gave to sell the package is paid on every hour once all of them are delivered, and if your gym or studio charges a flat per-session fee, that fee is owed on the makeup too.

Why does a flat facility fee hurt a discounted package more than full price?

A flat fee is the same dollar amount no matter what you billed the client, so it is a bigger percentage of a discounted package session than of a full-price single session. A $12 fee is 16% of a $75 session and nearly 21% of a $58 package-equivalent session — your own discount and the gym's flat cut compound against the same hour. A percentage revenue-share cut does not do this: it takes the same share of both, so it scales the comparison down without changing which side wins.

So should I stop offering packages, or stop training at a commission gym?

This calculator does not tell you what pricing or venue arrangement to run — that depends on what keeps clients booking with you and what space is available. It tells you the arithmetic consequence of the numbers you enter so the tradeoff (guaranteed revenue vs. protected hourly take-home) is a choice you make on purpose.

What no-show rate should I use if I don't track one?

Use your best honest estimate from recent memory, or run the comparison at a couple of different rates (for example 5% and 20%) to see how sensitive the result is. The point is the relationship between your discount and your no-show rate, not a precise historical figure.

Is this scheduling software or tax advice?

No. It applies the numbers you enter to one representative block of sessions — it does not track which client owes a makeup, does not schedule anything, and is not tax, legal, or financial advice.

I already compare these in a spreadsheet — why use this instead?

A spreadsheet catches the revenue comparison fine. It usually misses the hours a makeup guarantee still owes on a missed session, and it rarely models a flat facility fee eating a bigger share of a discounted rate than of full price. See this calculator vs. a spreadsheet for a worked example.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

Most trainers who compare a prepaid session package against pay-per-session pricing do it with one spreadsheet line: package price against sessions times single-session rate. That line answers a revenue question. It usually misses two things at once: the hours a makeup-owed policy still costs you, and the disproportionate bite a flat facility fee takes out of a discounted package rate.

What each one is for

A spreadsheet is fine for the revenue comparison, and most trainers already have one: package price in one cell, sessions times single rate in another. What it leaves out, unless someone builds it in on purpose, is hours — a package with a makeup guarantee still owes every session eventually — and a flat venue fee's uneven bite, since a fixed dollar amount is a bigger percentage of a discounted rate than of a full one.

This calculator takes your single-session rate, package size and price, no-show rate, whether a miss earns a makeup, and your gym or studio's percentage cut or flat facility fee, and reports net revenue and net effective hourly pay for both models side by side, plus the package price that would clear a take-home target.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Which pricing model brings in more revenue?A spreadsheet answers this fine — it's one subtraction.
Which pricing model pays more net per hour actually worked?Only if the sheet also converts a makeup policy into hours and applies your venue's cost per session, which most don't. This calculator does both directly.
Does a flat facility fee cost more, in percentage terms, against a discounted package?Yes — this page's worked example below shows exactly that case.
Does either one tell me what to charge?Neither. Both apply only the numbers you enter.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Worked example: a $75 session, a 10-for-$580 package, 10% no-shows, makeup owed, $12 flat facility fee

A trainer bills $75 per single session, and sells a package of 10 sessions for $580 — a 22.67% per-session discount. From recent memory, about 10% of booked sessions are no-shows, and the trainer's package policy is to reschedule (not forfeit) a missed session. The gym charges a flat $12 facility fee for every session actually delivered, package or not.

Pay-per-sessionPackage
Client billings for this block$675.00$580.00
Facility fee owed$108.00$120.00
Net take-home$567.00$460.00
Hours actually worked9.0010.00
Net effective hourly pay$63.00/hr$46.00/hr

A revenue-only spreadsheet line sees $580 versus $675 and stops at "the package brings in less, but it's guaranteed up front." It never surfaces two sharper facts. First, because the missed session is made up rather than forfeited, the trainer works more hours for less money — the 22.67% discount is deeper than the 10% no-show rate it was meant to cover. Second, the flat $12 facility fee is only 16% of the $75 full rate but almost 21% of the $58 package-equivalent rate — the same fixed fee, charged on more hours, at a lower price, eats a bigger share of the discounted work. Net effective hourly pay ends up $46.00/hr on the package against $63.00/hr charging full price per session and letting a no-show simply free that slot.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet compare package pricing against pay-per-session?

It can compare revenue in one line: package price against sessions times single-session rate. What it usually does not do on its own is account for the hours a makeup guarantee still owes on a missed session, or the way a flat per-session facility fee takes a bigger percentage bite out of a discounted package rate than out of full price.

Why does a revenue-only comparison miss the real answer?

Because a package guarantees revenue but, with a makeup owed, does not reduce hours the way a pay-per-session no-show does — every hour is eventually worked at the discounted rate. And a flat venue fee is the same dollar amount regardless of what you billed, so it is a bigger share of a discounted package session than of a full-price one. A spreadsheet cell comparing two revenue totals sees neither difference.

What would I have to build into a spreadsheet to catch this?

A row for whether a missed session is made up or forfeited, a formula that converts that choice into hours actually worked, a row for your venue's cost structure (percentage or flat fee) applied per session worked, and net effective hourly pay for both pricing models from those numbers — then keep every formula correct every time a rate, discount, no-show rate, or venue arrangement changes. This calculator runs that model directly and shows net revenue and net effective hourly pay side by side.

Does either one tell me what to charge?

No. Both a spreadsheet and this calculator only compute the consequence of numbers you supply — your single-session rate, package size and price, no-show rate, makeup policy, and venue cost. Neither one knows your market or your clients; you decide what to charge.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is uploaded.
